title: Evolutionary game theory

definition.text: The use of game theory to study evolving populations of living things, modelling Darwinian competition as a contest between strategies.

facts.text: It began in 1973 with John Maynard Smith and George R. Price's formal treatment of animal contests as strategies.
Unlike classical game theory it does not need rational players, only inherited strategies whose success is tested by survival and reproduction.
It focuses on how strategies change over time, which depends on how common each competing strategy is in the population.
It has helped explain group selection, sexual selection, altruism, parental care, co-evolution and ecological dynamics.
It began from the puzzle of why animals fight in restrained, ritualized ways over resources.
Life's problems of getting food, surviving and reproducing resemble economic problems of resource management, competitive strategy and investment, which is why game theory fits biology so well.

title: Evolutionarily stable strategy
article: Evolutionary game theory#The evolutionarily stable strategy

definition.text: A strategy that, once common in a large population, cannot be invaded by any rare mutant strategy.

facts.text: It is akin to the Nash equilibrium of classical game theory, but with stricter mathematical conditions.
A successful strategy must be able to spread when rare and to hold its ground once common.
In the hawk–dove game the evolutionarily stable strategy is a mixed one.
The rock-paper-scissors game played by male side-blotched lizards has no evolutionarily stable strategy, only endless cycles around a Nash equilibrium.

title: Bourgeois strategy
article: Evolutionary game theory#Asymmetries that allow new strategies

definition.text: An evolutionary strategy that settles contests by using some asymmetry between the rivals, such as who already holds the resource.

facts.text: It can beat a bluffing strategy in the war of attrition when such an asymmetry exists.
In the hawk–dove game, treating one player as territory owner and the other as intruder makes role-based strategies stable.

title: Evolution of altruism

definition.text: The puzzle, noted by Darwin, of how behaviour that helps another at a cost to oneself can survive natural selection, and the game-theory routes that explain it.

facts.text: If selection acts only on individuals, altruism makes no sense, yet many social animals behave altruistically.
Kin selection explains it through shared genes; Hamilton's rule says relatedness must exceed the ratio of cost to benefit.
Direct reciprocity ('I'll scratch your back if you scratch mine') and indirect reciprocity are further routes.
Without some measure of reputation, only direct reciprocity can arise in the prisoner's dilemma.

contested_note: Nowak and Wilson's group-selection explanation of insect eusociality challenges the kin-selection account and is described as controversial.

title: Rock paper scissors dynamics in nature

definition.text: Evolutionary games in which each strategy beats one rival and loses to another, so the strategies' shares cycle instead of settling down.

facts.text: Male side-blotched lizards have three throat-colour types with different mating strategies that beat one another in a circle.
Together with density effects in females, this drives a four-year population cycle.
The cyclic behaviour predicted by evolutionary game theory has also been seen in human laboratory experiments.

title: Coevolutionary games

definition.text: Evolutionary game dynamics that combine competition within a species with competition between species.

facts.text: Examples include predator–prey competition, host–parasite co-evolution and mutualism.
They add a third kind of dynamic beyond games that settle at a stable strategy and games that cycle.

title: Spatial games

definition.text: Evolutionary game models that place players on a grid so that each contest is only with immediate neighbours.

facts.text: Winning strategies take over local neighbourhoods and then spread into adjacent ones.

definition.text: A way of describing a game as a tree that shows the order of moves, each player's choices at each point, what they know when they choose, and the payoffs at the end.

facts.text: It gives a fuller description than the normal form, which reduces a game to a payoff matrix.
Normal form is generally used for simultaneous games and extensive form for sequential ones; it is a many-player version of a decision tree.
Each end point (leaf) of the tree lists one payoff for every player, and a play is a path from the root to a leaf.
Chance events are modelled as moves by a fictitious player called Nature, whose branches carry probabilities.
Such games are solved by backward induction, working from the end nodes back to the root.
Harold W. Kuhn gave the general definition in 1953, extending one by von Neumann from 1928.

definition.text: A game has perfect information when every player always knows everything that has happened so far, and imperfect information when some earlier move is hidden.

facts.text: Moves may be unobserved because they are simultaneous or hidden.
A game with any information set of more than one node has imperfect information.
An information set is drawn as a dotted line or a loop joining the nodes the player cannot tell apart.

definition.text: The device of turning a game of incomplete information, where players do not know others' payoffs or types, into one of complete but imperfect information by letting Nature choose the types.

facts.text: For example, Nature might pick a job applicant's ability as low with probability 1/3 or high with probability 2/3, and the employer does not see the pick.
Nature has no payoffs and its choice is drawn as an unfilled node.
